---
title: "Checks Internals"
---

Two functions turn a fit into a judgement. `verdicts()` reads each edge
indicator's inclusion Bayes factor as one of three verdicts and says whether a
rerun of the sampler could change it. `calibration_check()` asks whether the
model's conditional predictions land where they claim to. A third piece of
machinery sits behind the prior sensitivity check: the anchored curve, which
turns a handful of fits at fixed prior scales into a continuous curve without
refitting in between.

The three live in `R/verdicts.R`, `R/calibration_check.R`, and
`R/anchor_curve.R`. For argument lists and return formats, see
[Checking Tools](../reference/checks.qmd) in the Reference. This page documents
the estimators.

## The three-way rule

The decision rule itself is four lines. Write $\ell$ for the natural log
inclusion Bayes factor of an indicator and $t$ for the evidence threshold. With
$\lambda = \log t$:

$$
\text{verdict} =
\begin{cases}
\text{presence} & \ell \ge \lambda \\
\text{absence} & \ell \le -\lambda \\
\text{undecided} & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
$$

A missing Bayes factor gives a missing verdict rather than "undecided", which
matters for indicators that were never updated. The threshold is validated to
be a single finite number greater than one, so the two boundaries are always
on opposite sides of zero, and the same rule serves `verdicts()` and the
per-anchor verdicts of the sensitivity check.

The Bayes factor comes from
[`extract_inclusion_bf()`](../reference/extractors.qmd#extract_inclusion_bf),
read on the natural log scale. Working in logs is not cosmetic here: `log_bf`
stays finite where `bf` saturates at zero or infinity, and the fragility
machinery below needs a finite number to measure distances with.

`verdicts()` requires selection to have been on. Without it every edge is in
the model and there is no inclusion Bayes factor to read, so the function stops
with that explanation rather than returning an empty table.

### Reading the indicators in the right order

The verdict table is one row per indicator, in the order the raw indicator
draws lay them out, and that order is not the same for every model. A GGM or
ordinal fit lays its indicators out as the row-major upper triangle of the
variable order. A mixed fit lays them out by block, discrete by discrete first,
then continuous by continuous, then the cross block, which is a different
permutation whenever the discrete and continuous columns interleave in the
original data. `indicator_pair_index()` recovers the right one by filling the
mixed layout with draw positions and reading the positions back off, so the
Bayes factors and inclusion probabilities are looked up out of their symmetric
matrices at the positions the draws actually used.

`bgmCompare()` has its own layout again: for each variable, that variable's
main-effect difference on the diagonal followed by its pairwise differences,
which is what `compare_indicator_index()` builds.

## The fragility flag

A verdict near a boundary can flip on a rerun purely through Monte Carlo noise.
The flag makes that a per-edge statement rather than a caveat in the prose.

**The operating point.** In a known-truth calibration study of 37,010 graded
edge-fits across ordinal, binary, and Gaussian graphical models, all 66 verdict
errors sat within 0.58 of a threshold on the log Bayes factor scale, and no
edge further out was ever misclassified. Verdict error is therefore a boundary
phenomenon, and the flag marks the boundary region: an edge is fragile when a
verdict boundary lies within two standard errors of its estimated evidence.

**Two standard errors, because neither is enough alone.** Both are standard
errors of the logit inclusion probability, which is the log inclusion Bayes
factor scale shifted by the constant prior inclusion odds, so they are directly
comparable with $\ell$.

The *two-state* standard error, `two_state_se_logit()`, models each binary
indicator chain as a first-order two-state Markov chain. It counts within-chain
transitions only, never across the join between chains, and applies Jeffreys
smoothing to the transition rates:

$$
\hat a = \frac{n_{01} + \tfrac12}{n_0 + 1}, \qquad
\hat b = \frac{n_{10} + \tfrac12}{n_1 + 1}.
$$

The smoothing is what keeps the estimate defined at zero flips, where the
unsmoothed rates would be $0/0$. From $\hat a$ and $\hat b$ the routine forms
the stationary probability $p = \hat a / (\hat a + \hat b)$ and the two-state
effective sample size, and returns $1/\sqrt{\text{ESS}\,p(1-p)}$. On its own
this standard error caught 74% of the study's verdict errors.

The *Rao-Blackwellized* standard error, `rb_se_logit()`, takes the Monte Carlo
standard error of the one-step inclusion draws (see
[GGM Internals](ggm-internals.qmd#rao-blackwellized-inclusion-draws)) to the
logit scale by the delta method, multiplying by $1/(p(1-p))$. It is `NA`
wherever the incoming MCSE is, which is where the draws are constant to double
precision. On its own it caught 94%.

**The union rule.** `boundary_distance()` divides the gap to the nearer
boundary, $\min(|\ell - \lambda|, |\ell + \lambda|)$, by each standard error,
and an edge is fragile when either distance falls below 2. A missing distance
abstains rather than votes. The union caught all 66 errors at the cost of
flagging 3.0% of correct verdicts, and it transfers across model types, so the
same operating point serves Gaussian graphical models as it serves ordinal and
binary ones.

A fragile verdict is not a wrong verdict. It is a verdict the run was too short
to settle, and the remedy is more iterations.

**Where the flag is not calibrated.** Every arm of the study fitted a single
network. On `bgmCompare()` difference indicators the same arithmetic runs and
still marks verdicts near a boundary, but no study has measured what share of
difference-verdict errors it catches or how many correct verdicts it rejects.
The returned object carries `flag_validated = FALSE` for those fits and the
print method says so in plain language, alongside a second caveat that
difference verdicts are contingent on `difference_scale`, whose default
calibration is under study.

`verdicts()` draws no random numbers. Given a fit and a threshold it is
deterministic, and there is no `seed` argument.

### The reporting cap

`format_log_bf()` prints a rounded value inside a cap of $10^4$ and an
inequality outside it. Past the cap the digits carry no information a longer
run would reproduce, and a saturated Bayes factor has no value to print at all.
A log Bayes factor that rounds to zero prints as `0`, never `-0.0`: the sign of
a rounded-away quantity is not something the run established.

## Calibration

`calibration_check()` asks a different question: not whether an edge is there,
but whether the model's predictions are honest. The unit is the conditional
distribution $P(x_{ij} \mid \text{the rest of case } i)$, which is the model's
own regression unit, so the check runs one variable at a time. Pooling across
variables would let miscalibrations in opposite directions cancel.

### Discrete variables

For every case and every category threshold the model issues a cumulative
probability and the data record whether the case fell at or below it. Isotonic
regression, through `stats::isoreg()`, estimates the observed frequency as a
monotone function of the predicted probability, and a calibrated variable
tracks the diagonal. The final cumulative probability is 1 for every case and
is dropped, since it says nothing about calibration.

The predictions are the posterior-mean ones from
[`predict()`](simulation-prediction.qmd#predicting-conditional-distributions).

**The consistency band.** The band answers "how far from the diagonal does a
model that is calibrated by construction wander on data this size?" It is built
by simulation: for each of `nrep` replicates, `pav_panels()` draws one
*category* per case from that case's own predicted distribution by inverse CDF,
recomputes the isotonic curve, and takes pointwise quantiles of the result.

Resampling the category rather than the threshold events is the load-bearing
choice. One case's cumulative threshold events are nested by construction, and
resampling them independently would produce a band that is too narrow, making
ordinary wander look like miscalibration.

### Continuous variables

A continuous variable's prediction is a density, so there is no category to
have fallen in. The same question is asked through the probability integral
transform: $u_{ij} = F_j(y_{ij} \mid y_{i,-j})$ is Uniform(0, 1) exactly when
the conditional predictive distribution is right. The panel is the empirical
distribution function of the $u$ values against the uniform diagonal.

`conditional_pit()` builds $F_j$ as the predictive mixture over `ndraws`
posterior draws,

$$
u_{ij} = \frac{1}{D} \sum_{d=1}^{D}
  \Phi\!\left( \frac{y_{ij} - m_{ij}^{(d)}}{s_{ij}^{(d)}} \right),
$$

using the internal `return_draws` path of the prediction helpers so it receives
the per-draw conditional parameters instead of their average. Parameter
uncertainty therefore sits inside the distribution the observation is
transformed by. A single draw's Gaussian would be too narrow by exactly the
amount the posterior is uncertain, and the uniform reference would no longer be
the right one.

**Its band is not resampled from the model.** Under the transform the null is
Uniform(0, 1) whatever the conditional density was, so `uniform_ecdf_band()`
simulates the empirical distribution functions of $n$ independent uniforms and
takes pointwise quantiles. It depends on $n$ alone, which is why one band
serves every continuous variable in a fit.

The two panel kinds therefore condition on different things: the isotonic panel
on posterior-mean probabilities, the transform panel on the full predictive
distribution. Both live on the unit square against the diagonal, so a mixed fit
produces one figure and one summary table, with a `kind` column recording which
construction produced each row.

### What is seeded

Both bands consume random numbers from R's own generator, and `seed` is the
only control over them: `calibration_check()` calls `set.seed()` when `seed` is
supplied and does nothing otherwise. Because the selection of posterior draws
for the predictive mixture also goes through R's generator, one seed fixes the
whole check. Leave `seed` unset and the summary numbers move a little between
calls, by the width of the band's own Monte Carlo error.

### Per group

On a `bgmCompare()` fit the check runs per group. A group's cases are the ones
its own parameters predict, so pooling them would let a variable predicted too
high in one group cancel against another, exactly as pooling variables would.
Every variable in a comparison fit is discrete, so every panel is isotonic, and
`ndraws` has no effect because `predict.bgmCompare()` issues posterior-mean
predictions only.

The row alignment is worth stating, because it is a real trap. The fit stores
its cases sorted by group, so the membership vector the check uses is in that
internal order. Supplied `newdata` arrives in the order the data were given and
is permuted by the same stable sort before use, which is why the method insists
on one row per fitted case in the original order rather than accepting an
arbitrary matrix.

### What the check does not say

Evaluated on the fitted data the check is in-sample: the observation entered
the parameters it is judged against, so the transform is mildly
under-dispersed and the check is conservative. Held-out `newdata` removes that
and makes it strictly harder to pass.

More important, calibrated conditional predictions do not imply that the model
reproduces the joint distribution. A model can predict each variable well from
the others and still understate how strongly they depend on one another. That
question needs a display built on [`simulate()`](simulation-prediction.qmd).

## The anchored curve

`R/anchor_curve.R` is the estimator behind the prior sensitivity check's
continuous curve. The check refits the model at a handful of fixed slab scales,
the anchors; this file fills in everything between them without refitting.
[Sensitivity and Refits](sensitivity-refit.qmd) documents the grid, the refits,
and the gate that decides which anchors are allowed to contribute.

### Reweighting

Take a fit at anchor scale $s_a$ and ask what its posterior would have been at
a nearby scale $s$. Only the slab prior on the currently included edges
changes, so the likelihood cancels, the spike terms cancel, and a fixed-scale
anchor has no scale posterior to integrate. What is left is a per-draw ratio of
slab densities. `anchor_log_weights()` forms its logarithm over the included
edges, with $m_t$ the number of included edges in draw $t$:

$$
\log w_t(s) = -m_t \log\frac{s}{s_a}
  - \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{1}{s^2} - \frac{1}{s_a^2} \right)
    \sum_{e:\,\gamma_{te}=1} \theta_{te}^2
$$

for a Normal slab, and the matching sum of $\log(1 + (\theta/s)^2)$ differences
for a Cauchy one. This is the posterior-density-ratio reweighting identity of
@BartosEtAl_2026_sensitivity, applied locally around each anchor; the anchored
construction that stitches the anchors together is specific to `bgms`.

`anchor_draws()` supplies $\theta$ in the frame the slab prior applies to,
which for a GGM fit means the precision draws carry the $-\tfrac12$ factor
first. For a `bgmCompare()` fit one indicator can gate several parameters: a
pairwise difference indicator gates that pair's difference in every contrast,
and a main-effect difference indicator gates the whole block of that variable's
threshold differences in every contrast. `compare_anchor_draws()` builds the
ownership map, so the weight sums over gated parameters while the inclusion
probability stays reported per indicator.

`anchor_reweight()` then does self-normalized importance sampling at each
target scale, both pooled across chains and per chain, and records the
importance effective sample size $(\sum w)^2 / \sum w^2$ alongside each
estimate.

### Stitching

`assemble_curve()` builds the displayed curve one grid point at a time. Every
anchor whose importance ESS at that point clears `ess_floor`, and which passed
its own convergence gate, contributes its reweighted inclusion probability,
weighted by inverse variance on that scale:

$$
w_a = \frac{\text{ESS}_a}{\max\!\left(p_a(1 - p_a),\, 10^{-6}\right)}.
$$

The clamp keeps a saturated edge from dividing by zero. Pooling happens on the
inclusion-probability scale and is transformed to the log Bayes factor
afterwards, which is what removes the staircase seams and the infinities that
winner-take-all anchor selection produced at hand-off points: a capped-edge
anchor no longer hands off discontinuously to a finite one.

Grid points where no anchor clears the floor are masked to `NA` rather than
extrapolated. Each surviving point is tagged with its highest-ESS anchor for
reporting, and at an anchor's own grid position that tag is the anchor itself.
The per-chain curves pool with the same weights, so the downstream per-point
Monte Carlo standard error and chain-unanimity checks carry over unchanged.

The pooled rows are an approximation and are treated as one. Exactness lives on
the anchor fits' own Rao-Blackwellized statistics: the per-anchor verdict
columns and every chosen-scale quantity are read straight from each fit, so the
`1x` column is exactly the original fit's reported analysis. This is the
multistate-bridge direction; fully self-consistent weights are future work.
